Pregnancy

Ultrasound at 29 weeks: purpose, findings and follow-up

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A scan around 29 weeks can answer a particular question about your baby or pregnancy. It is not a compulsory appointment for everyone, and a reassuring picture cannot answer every question about health. Knowing why the examination was requested makes the report and the next steps easier to understand.

Is a scan at 29 weeks routine?

Schedules vary between health services and according to individual needs. For example, NICE does not recommend routine scans after 28 weeks for uncomplicated singleton pregnancies. Other services use different pathways. A scan at this stage should have a clear purpose rather than be booked simply because the calendar reaches week 29.

Your team may arrange one because growth measurements raise a concern, an earlier scan needs follow-up, or a condition affecting you or your baby calls for closer monitoring. Ask what question the scan will answer, what it includes and who will explain the result. You can discuss the benefits, limits and your choices.

Reasons for an earlier or additional assessment

An ultrasound may help investigate suspected changes in growth or amniotic fluid, check a previously low placenta, or assess a pregnancy with particular medical risks. A focused examination answers a narrower question than a detailed structural or specialist examination; the word ‘scan’ does not describe one identical test.

Reduced movements, bleeding, leaking fluid, contractions, an abdominal injury or a potentially harmful exposure need prompt clinical advice. Assessment can include examination, heart-rate monitoring or blood and urine tests as well as ultrasound. Do not arrange a routine scan and wait for it when symptoms need attention now.

What might your baby look like?

At 29 weeks, development, fat accumulation and organ maturation are continuing. The NHS describes an approximate head-to-heel length of 38.6 cm as a guide to this stage. It is not a required target or a length usually measured directly on a late-pregnancy scan; babies differ and growth is assessed with other measurements.

Bones commonly look bright or white and fluid looks dark. You may see movement or breathing-like movements, depending on position and the observation period. The picture does not measure muscle strength, and seeing breathing movements does not prove that the lungs are ready for birth. Seeing the genitals also depends on the views obtained and is not the main purpose of a clinical scan.

The appointment, preparation and duration

Usually, gel is placed on the abdomen and a probe is moved over the skin. If a more accurate view of the cervix or the relationship between the placenta and cervix is needed, the team may discuss a vaginal scan and seek your consent. Follow the clinic’s preparation instructions; do not assume that fasting or a full bladder is always necessary.

Many ultrasound appointments take about 20–30 minutes, but this is not a maximum. The baby’s position, the clinical question and incomplete views can mean more time or another appointment. A biophysical profile or separate heart-rate monitoring may add time. Tell the examiner if you feel uncomfortable and ask how and when the report will be discussed.

Growth measurements are estimates

The examiner may measure the head, abdomen and thigh bone and use these to estimate weight. The result is compared with a growth chart and the rest of the clinical picture. Estimated weight has uncertainty: one small or large measurement is not, by itself, a diagnosis or a reason to decide on delivery.

Previous measurements, the interval between scans, fluid and sometimes blood-flow measurements help the team interpret a growth concern. A due date established reliably earlier in pregnancy is generally not changed because a late scan estimates a different size. Ask whether the finding needs follow-up and what change the team is watching for.

Position, fluid, placenta, cervix and cord

A scan can show the baby’s current position, estimate the amount of amniotic fluid and assess placental location. Position at 29 weeks does not necessarily predict position at birth. Low or high fluid needs interpretation in context. If placental location or an earlier history raises concern, a specialist may assess whether the placenta is abnormally attached to the womb wall; this is not a diagnosis made from a routine picture alone.

Placental calcification or a reported ‘grade’ describes appearance and cannot on its own establish how well the placenta works. Cervical assessment is used when it answers a clinical question. Some cord features may be seen, but a scan cannot reliably exclude every loop, true knot or other cord problem. An apparent cord finding needs clinical interpretation, not a diagnosis from a keepsake image.

When Doppler adds information

Doppler ultrasound assesses blood flow in selected vessels. It may be useful when the team is investigating growth or placental concerns, for example. Which vessels are examined and how the results are interpreted depend on the reason for testing and the stage of pregnancy.

Doppler is not required for every 29-week appointment, and colour on a screen is not proof that a scan is more thorough. The result is considered with growth, fluid, heart-rate assessment and your circumstances. Ask what a Doppler finding changes about monitoring or care rather than trying to interpret a number alone.

What is a biophysical profile?

A full biophysical profile combines an assessment of the fetal heart-rate response, usually a non-stress test, with ultrasound observations of breathing movements, body movements, muscle tone and amniotic fluid. A modified profile generally combines the non-stress test with a fluid assessment. The exact examination offered should be explained to you.

This is a selected wellbeing assessment, not a universal test at 29 weeks. Sleep, medicines, gestational age and the observation period can affect findings. A non-reactive heart-rate test or a particular score does not tell you the whole story on its own. The team decides whether more observation, repeat or additional testing, specialist advice or delivery planning is appropriate.

What 2D, 3D and 4D images cannot guarantee

Standard two-dimensional ultrasound is the basis of clinical assessment. Three-dimensional views and moving 3D images, often called 4D, can help answer selected questions, but a lifelike face image is not a more complete health check. Position, gestational age and technical factors can limit views, and ultrasound cannot identify every structural or genetic condition.

Ultrasound uses sound waves rather than X-rays. It should be performed by trained professionals for a medical purpose, using the exposure needed to obtain useful information. Extra or prolonged scanning solely for souvenir images is discouraged. A normal result is reassuring within the examination’s scope, rather than a guarantee that nothing can be wrong.

If a heartbeat is not heard

Not hearing sound during a scan does not mean that the baby has died. The examiner can assess and document cardiac movement visually without playing an audible heartbeat. A home Doppler, a missing sound or a photograph cannot confirm or exclude a serious problem.

If the clinical team cannot identify cardiac activity, urgent assessment with appropriate ultrasound and confirmation by a qualified clinician, including a second opinion, are needed. Technical difficulties must be considered. If a loss is confirmed, the team should explain it clearly and compassionately and discuss care and birth options according to your health and circumstances.

Understanding an incomplete or unexpected result

Sometimes a view is incomplete rather than abnormal. Sometimes a measurement or finding needs review because its meaning is uncertain. Depending on the question, the next step may be another scan, specialist fetal-medicine assessment, other tests or a monitoring plan. There is no single repeat interval or treatment suitable for every finding.

Before leaving, ask what was seen, what remains uncertain, who will review the report and when you should hear from them. Ask what symptoms should bring you back sooner. A finding is not evidence that you caused it, and you do not need to interpret the images yourself to take part in decisions.

When to seek help without waiting for a scan

Contact your maternity team immediately if movements are less than usual, stop or change from your baby’s usual pattern; do not wait until the next day or use a home Doppler for reassurance. Also contact maternity care promptly for bleeding, a gush or trickle of fluid, regular contractions or period-like pain before 37 weeks, or after a fall or direct blow to the abdomen. A recent reassuring scan does not replace assessment of new symptoms.

Use emergency care for heavy bleeding, bleeding with severe abdominal or shoulder pain, dizziness or fainting, or if you are seriously unwell. Suspected poisoning or a harmful exposure needs urgent poison-service or medical advice; if a harmful substance may have been swallowed, inhaled or touched, seek emergency advice rather than waiting for ultrasound. Do not induce vomiting, and keep the packaging for the team. Do not drive yourself if faint or seriously unwell.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

This guide explains a clinically indicated late-pregnancy scan, not a universal screening schedule.

Growth, placental appearance, Doppler and wellbeing tests require interpretation in their clinical context.

Further tests and follow-up depend on the specific findings, local pathway and your preferences.

How BeMama can help

BeMama brings the appointment, report and follow-up questions together so you can discuss them with your maternity team.

When to seek help

This information cannot diagnose a problem or replace maternity assessment. Seek prompt care for changed movements or warning symptoms; a reassuring image is not a reason to delay.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A 29-week scan should answer a clinical question; schedules and individual needs vary.
  • Growth estimates, fluid, placenta and blood flow are interpreted together, not from one picture or number.
  • Doppler and biophysical profiles are selected tests, not compulsory extras for everyone.
  • An unheard heartbeat is not a diagnosis; suspected absent cardiac activity needs qualified ultrasound confirmation.
  • Reduced movements or new warning symptoms need prompt care even after a reassuring scan.

Frequently asked questions

Why might I need an ultrasound at 29 weeks?

To follow growth, fluid or placental concerns, clarify a previous finding or monitor a particular risk. Ask which question your scan is intended to answer. Symptoms needing urgent care should be assessed promptly rather than waiting for the appointment.

Will it be finished within 30 minutes?

Often a scan takes around 20–30 minutes, but difficult views, specialist assessment, a biophysical profile or heart-rate monitoring can take longer. Your clinic can explain the planned examination.

Does not hearing a heartbeat mean the baby has died?

No. Cardiac movement may be assessed without audible sound. If activity cannot be identified clinically, urgent appropriate ultrasound and qualified confirmation, including a second opinion, are needed.

What happens if the scan finds a problem?

The team explains what is known and uncertain and may arrange repeat imaging, additional tests, specialist review or a care plan. The finding and your circumstances determine timing; there is no automatic next step for every abnormal result.

Can this scan change my due date?

A due date reliably established earlier is generally not changed because a later scan measures a different size. Late measurements are mainly used to assess growth and guide care.

Do I need a 4D scan?

Not routinely. Standard 2D imaging provides the basis of assessment; 3D or 4D may help with a specific question. A lifelike image cannot rule out every condition or replace the clinical report.

Must I fast or arrive with a full bladder?

Follow your own clinic’s instructions. Preparation depends on the examination, and neither fasting nor a full bladder should be assumed to be a universal requirement.

Can a normal scan explain away reduced movements?

No. Contact maternity care immediately for reduced, stopped or changed movements, even if a recent scan was reassuring. Do not wait overnight or rely on a home Doppler.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
